accepted_phrases: General pages describe cocoa seeds being fermented for flavor development, dried, cleaned and roasted; shells are removed to reveal nibs, which are ground into chocolate liquor. Chocolate liquor is nonalcoholic cocoa mass made by grinding fermented, dried, roasted and skinned nibs until cocoa butter is released, and it contains both cocoa solids and cocoa butter. This chain explains process stages but does not establish the exact roast, fermentation, liquor composition, bean origin or process control of any captured seller offer.

One New Jersey author planned a blind comparison of milk-chocolate-covered caramels from eight local shops but the packet contains no results and the products are not the five exact bars. New Haven posters offered place- and time-specific hot-cocoa preferences and one author explicitly noted cold weather could have affected satisfaction. An ELI5 discussion says aroma, texture, temperature and visual cues contribute to flavor, but it is a lay forum discussion. These pages motivate masking, standard temperature, equal form-specific portions and local preference records; they do not rank exact offers or establish a universal tasting method.

Conching uses mixing and agitation to distribute cocoa butter, coat particles, release volatile acids, reduce moisture and develop texture and flavor. Its duration depends on batch size and equipment; modern large batches can be processed much faster than traditional ones. Therefore conching matters, but a longer time is not automatically superior and no frozen seller page supplies a verified conching time, equipment, temperature or matched sensory effect for its exact bar.

Conditional title arithmetic makes the Green & Black's pack about 2.87 dollars per nominal bar and about 0.91 dollars per nominal ounce only if eight times 3.17 ounces is the delivered total; the Product Dimensions field creates an unresolved conflict. The Lindt milk listing is 4.79 dollars per nominal piece only if two pieces are delivered, but the 4.4-ounce field does not establish whether it is total or per piece. The Chocolove listing is about 4.50 dollars per nominal bar only if two bars are delivered, while its total mass remains unresolved. Lindt white lacks a stated mass. Ritter is about 2.27 dollars per declared ounce. These calculations expose assumptions and cannot rank unlike categories or replace current delivered-price verification.

A percentage or category name is incomplete without its component basis and exact recipe. Cocoa liquor contains cocoa solids and cocoa butter, white chocolate uses cocoa butter without non-fat cocoa solids, milk products and added ingredients alter form, and the mixed pack contains multiple categories including an almond product. Percentage can be recorded literally, but 85, 70 or 61 cannot by itself rank bitterness, sweetness, aroma, texture, processing quality, price value or guest preference across unlike products.

The five seller pages freeze offer assertions rather than current delivered labels or taste results. Green & Black's SKU B08M4XT3XM is 22.98 dollars with no reviews shown; its title and detail describe eight 3.17-ounce bars allocated across 85-percent dark, 70-percent dark, milk-with-almonds, milk and white, while Product Dimensions reports 3.17 ounces and the selected flavor field says 70-percent cacao. Lindt white SKU B07938SPXM is 5.39 dollars with no reviews and no mass shown. Lindt milk SKU B01N3OYUMS is 9.58 dollars with no reviews, titled 4.4 ounces and two pieces while Product Dimensions reports 4.4 ounces. Ritter SKU B07PRJC1KW is 7.99 dollars, rated 55 percent over four reviews, for one 61-percent 100-gram or 3.52-ounce bar. Chocolove ruby SKU B07SQ4JSKK is 8.99 dollars, rated 78 percent over twelve reviews, titled two bars and selected as a 3.1-ounce two-pack while Product Dimensions reports 3.1 ounces. None proves a current delivered total, complete formula, allergen status or guest preference.

White chocolate is described as cocoa butter, sugar and milk solids without non-fat cocoa solids; it is still presented as one traditional chocolate type, while consumers dispute the name and legal composition standards vary by market. Ruby chocolate is described as a pink or purple style introduced as a distinct product, while experts debate whether a fourth natural type is real or marketing. These pages defeat a universal fake-versus-real slogan but do not independently classify the exact Lindt white or Chocolove ruby offers without current ingredients, cocoa components, market and label verification.

A category contrast can teach guests about forms, while only matched products can support a narrower price or quality comparison, and all results remain local to these guests, lots and conditions.

The packet proves no universal percentage ladder, no automatic process premium and no fake-versus-real verdict.
